etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gentil (“courteous, noble”), from Old French gentil (“high-born, noble”), from Latin gentilis (“of the same family or clan”), from gens (“[Roman] clan”). Doublet of gentile, genteel, and jaunty.

definitions.definition: Tender and amiable; of a considerate or kindly disposition.
Soft and mild rather than hard or severe.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 3, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: Here the stripped panelling was warmly gold and the pictures, mostly of the English school, were mellow and gentle in the afternoon light.

definitions.definition: Gradual rather than steep or sudden.
Polite and respectful rather than rude.
(archaic) Well-born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.

quote.citation: 1822, [Walter Scott], Peveril of the Peak. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), Edinburgh:  […]  Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Hurst, Robinson, and Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: "You are of gentle blood," she said  […]

quote.citation: 1893-1897, Charles Kendall Adams (editor), Johnson's Universal Encyclopedia
quote.text: British society is divided into nobility, gentry, and yeomanry, and families are either noble, gentle, or simple.

quote.citation: [1644], [John Milton], Of Education. To Master Samuel Hartlib, [London:  […]  Thomas Underhill and/or Thomas Johnson], →OCLC:
quote.text: the studies wherein our noble and gentle youth ought to bestow their time

quote.citation: 2013, Kathryn L.M. Reynolds, Garland Roses, Kathryn L.M. Reynolds, →ISBN, page 226:
quote.text: “She's experienced a horrific and nasty scare and is in a state of shock, but otherwise she's relatively okay.” Conrad replied, his tone at first grim (as he recalled what he'd seen in the family room) and then it gentled to a more doctorial tone as he directed his next comments to his patient.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:

definitions.definition: (transitive, animal husbandry) To break; to tame; to domesticate.

quote.citation: 2008, Frank Leslie, The Killing Breed, Penguin, →ISBN:
quote.text: Yakima could have tried to catch him, gentle him as Wolf had been gentled, but having two stallions in his cavvy would lead to a different kind of trouble.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To soothe; to calm; to make gentle.

quote.citation: 1996, William C. Loring, An American Romantic-realist Abroad: Templeton Strong and His Music, Scarecrow Press, →ISBN, page 201:
quote.text: A hornist, his playing gentled by perspective, is out of sight within the woods, but his notes are heard through or over the murmuring mix of bird song and breeze in leaves.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
2012, Lizzie Stark, Leaving Mundania: Inside the Transformative World of Live Action Role-Playing Games, Chicago Review Press, →ISBN, page 43:
quote.text: While actual medieval societies were full of lots of peasants and a few rich and noble gentles, SCA personas tend to be nobles rather than commoners.

definitions.definition: (fishing) A maggot used as bait by anglers.

quote.citation: 1846, Douglas William Jerrold, “The History of St. Giles and St. James”, in (Please provide the book title or journal name):
quote.text: Pooh! the whole thing is as alive and wrigging as an angler's box of gentles
Years ago, on Victoria's Port Phillip Bay, the recognised bait for garfish were `gentles', a genteel word for maggots, which were especially grown for gar fishermen.
